title: Biodiversity Register — Chapter Summary
intro: Look closely at any school plot and you will find dozens of living things — sparrows, mango trees, ants, lichens, frogs after rain. The variety of all this life is BIODIVERSITY. A BIODIVERSITY REGISTER is a careful notebook in which you record what lives in a place, where you saw it, when, and what it does. This chapter teaches you to observe quietly, sketch what you see, gather information from many sources, and turn it all into a poster or presentation. By doing so you train your scientific eye — and the register itself becomes a small, real act of conservation.

sections.heading: What Biodiversity Is
bullets: Bio (life) + diversity (variety) → variety of life on Earth.
Three levels: SPECIES (different kinds), GENETIC (varieties within a species), ECOSYSTEM (different kinds of places).
India is one of the most biodiverse countries — roughly 1 lakh known species.
Even your school yard hosts dozens of species — birds, plants, insects, lichens, microbes.

sections.heading: What a Biodiversity Register Is
bullets: A careful record of the living things in a chosen area, made by people who live there.
Each entry: place, habitat, living-thing name (local + scientific), description, date / time, source.
A school register might cover the campus and a 100 m radius.
People's Biodiversity Registers are kept by Biodiversity Management Committees in many panchayats.

sections.heading: Where to Look — Habitats
bullets: Trees and bushes — birds, squirrels, lichens, insects.
Ground — ants, beetles, spiders, frogs after rain.
Soil — earthworms, microbes (root partners of plants).
Walls and stones — gecko lizards, spiders, mosses, lichens.
Water — pondweed, tadpoles, water-striders, algae.
Visit each habitat at different times of day.

sections.heading: How to Observe and Record
bullets: Be quiet for at least 2–3 minutes; let living things forget you.
Sketch + note colour, size, behaviour.
Record place, date, time, weather.
Use local + scientific name if known; mark uncertainty as 'possibly X'.
NEVER catch, hurt or remove living things — observe only.
Tools: pencil + small notebook, magnifying glass, measuring tape, field guide.

sections.heading: Sources and Sharing
bullets: Local people (farmers, elders) often know local names better than books.
Field guides, library books, reliable websites (iNaturalist, India Biodiversity Portal) help identification.
Always record WHERE each piece of information came from.
After 2–4 weeks, share findings: poster, slide deck, short talk.
Good presentations also raise NEW questions to investigate.
The register documents change and supports conservation arguments.

key_takeaways: Biodiversity = variety of life at species, genetic and ecosystem levels.
A biodiversity register is a careful record of what lives in a chosen area.
Each entry: place, habitat, living thing, description, date/time, source.
Visit different habitats — trees, ground, soil, walls, water, air — at different times of day.
Observe quietly, sketch, be honest about uncertainty, never catch or hurt.
Use local people, field guides and reliable websites as sources, and record every source.
Share via poster, slide deck or short talk; raise questions.
Recording biodiversity is itself a small, real act of conservation.

glossary.definition: The variety of life on Earth — including species, genetic and ecosystem variety.
The variety of different KINDS of plants, animals, fungi and microbes in an area.
The variety of different VARIETIES within a single species (e.g. basmati and sona masoori rice).
The variety of different KINDS OF PLACES — forests, rivers, deserts, coral reefs.
A careful notebook recording the living things in a chosen area, with descriptions, places and sources.
The kind of place where a living thing lives — soil, water, tree, wall, air.
An illustrated booklet that helps identify common plants, birds or insects of a region.
An official local register of biodiversity, maintained by a panchayat's Biodiversity Management Committee.
A living thing (often a bee or butterfly) that carries pollen between flowers, helping plants make seeds and fruit.
A useful effect that nature provides for free — pollination, pest control, fertile soil, clean air, cool shade.
Caring for and protecting living things and their habitats.
Careful, quiet watching of a living thing in the place where it lives, with notes and sketches.
In science, openly marking what you are not sure about, e.g. 'possibly a bulbul'.
A reliable app and website used to identify plants and animals from photos, with help from a global community.
A small living thing — a partnership of a fungus and an alga — often found on tree bark and walls.
